rules.title: The PostgreSQL systemd unit is enabled
rules.explanation: systemd unit files define how services start and stop on Linux systems that use systemd. The PostgreSQL service unit should be enabled so the database server starts automatically with the operating system.
rules.impact: If the PostgreSQL systemd unit is not enabled, the database may remain unavailable after a reboot or other system state change until an administrator starts it manually.
rules.scope: Settings in the systemd unit for PostgreSQL

rules.title: The PostgreSQL data cluster is initialized
rules.explanation: A PostgreSQL data cluster is a collection of databases managed by a single server instance and stored under the data directory (commonly referenced as $PGDATA). The cluster must be initialized with initdb (or an equivalent packaging step) before the server can store or serve data.
rules.impact: An uninitialized data cluster prevents PostgreSQL from starting as a usable database service. Without a valid cluster, applications cannot connect and security controls that depend on a running instance cannot be enforced.

rules.title: The postgres user umask is set correctly
rules.explanation: The umask permission mask controls the default mode of newly created files and directories. The postgres operating-system account should use a restrictive umask such as 077 so that only the file owner receives access by default.
rules.impact: A permissive default umask (for example 002) can leave files created by postgres readable or writable by other accounts. That exposure can disclose configuration, credentials, or scripts, or allow unauthorized modification of database-related files.

rules.title: Pg_wheel group membership is restricted
rules.explanation: The pg_wheel group is a host group used to grant selected accounts elevated access to PostgreSQL administration, typically through sudo to the postgres superuser. Only trusted administrators who require database cluster ownership privileges should be members of pg_wheel.
rules.impact: Unauthorized membership in pg_wheel can allow a user to assume postgres privileges, administer the cluster, and access scripts, configuration, and data files that should remain restricted.

rules.title: Log_destination is configured
rules.explanation: The log_destination GUC selects where PostgreSQL writes server log messages. Supported destinations include stderr, csvlog, and syslog (and eventlog on Windows). At least one destination must be configured for core server logging to be retained.
rules.impact: If log_destination is unset or empty, messages from core PostgreSQL processes may be discarded. Loss of those logs reduces visibility into authentication failures, errors, and other security-relevant events.

rules.title: Logging_collector is enabled
rules.explanation: The logging collector is a background process that captures log messages sent to stderr and writes them to files under log_directory. The logging_collector parameter enables that process and can be set only at server start.
rules.impact: Without the logging collector, stderr- and csvlog-based logging may not persist to managed log files. Some process and script errors (for example dynamic linker failures or archive_command output) can also be missed when collector-based logging is disabled.

rules.title: Log_directory is set correctly
rules.explanation: The log_directory GUC specifies where log files are written when log_destination includes stderr or csvlog. The path may be absolute or relative to the cluster data directory and should follow the organization's logging policy.
rules.impact: An incorrect or unset log_directory can prevent log files from being written, or can place logs in an unintended location. Misdirected logs reduce auditability and can interfere with monitoring and retention controls.

rules.title: Log_file_mode is set correctly
rules.explanation: The log_file_mode GUC sets the permission bits applied to files created by the logging collector. The value is a numeric mode in the form accepted by chmod and umask (octal values should begin with 0). A common setting is 0600 so only the server owner can read and write log files; 0640 may be used when group read access is required and logs are stored outside the data directory.
rules.impact: PostgreSQL log files can contain sensitive operational and query-related data. Overly permissive log_file_mode values increase the risk of unauthorized disclosure of that information.

rules.title: Syslog_facility is set correctly
rules.explanation: The syslog_facility GUC selects the syslog facility used when PostgreSQL logs to syslog. Typical choices are the LOCAL0 through LOCAL7 facilities. The facility should match the organization's syslog daemon configuration and logging policy.
rules.impact: An inappropriate facility can mix PostgreSQL messages with unrelated applications, misroute them through filtering rules, or cause them to be dropped depending on the system logger configuration.

rules.title: Log_min_messages is set correctly
rules.explanation: The log_min_messages GUC controls which message severities are written to the server log. Each level includes that severity and all more severe levels. Valid values range from DEBUG5 through PANIC; WARNING is commonly used unless organizational policy requires a different threshold.
rules.impact: A threshold that is too high can omit security-relevant warnings and errors. A threshold that is too low can flood logs with debug noise, obscure important events, and increase storage and processing cost.

rules.title: Debug_print_parse is disabled
rules.explanation: The debug_print_parse GUC prints the parse tree for each executed query at the LOG message level. Unless organizational logging policy explicitly requires this diagnostic output, the parameter should remain off.
rules.impact: Enabling debug print settings can write detailed query structure to the logs, including information that would otherwise be omitted. That increases the risk of sensitive data exposure through log files.

rules.title: Debug_print_rewritten is disabled
rules.explanation: The debug_print_rewritten GUC prints the query rewriter output for each executed query at the LOG message level. Unless organizational logging policy explicitly requires this diagnostic output, the parameter should remain off.
rules.impact: Enabling debug print settings can write detailed rewritten query text to the logs. That increases the risk of sensitive data exposure through log files.

rules.title: Debug_print_plan is disabled
rules.explanation: The debug_print_plan GUC prints the execution plan for each executed query at the LOG message level. Unless organizational logging policy explicitly requires this diagnostic output, the parameter should remain off.
rules.impact: Enabling debug print settings can write detailed plan information and related query context to the logs. That increases the risk of sensitive data exposure through log files.

rules.title: Log_connections is enabled
rules.explanation: The log_connections GUC records each attempted connection to the server and successful client authentication. The setting is fixed for the lifetime of a backend session and is typically paired with log_disconnections.
rules.impact: PostgreSQL does not otherwise retain a durable internal history of connection attempts for later review. Without connection logging, unexpected or failed access attempts are harder to detect and investigate.

rules.title: Log_disconnections is enabled
rules.explanation: The log_disconnections GUC records the end of each session, including session duration. The setting is fixed for the lifetime of a backend session and is typically paired with log_connections.
rules.impact: Without disconnection logging, session duration and orderly termination are not captured for audit. That reduces the ability to correlate connection start and end events or identify anomalous long-lived sessions.

rules.title: Log_error_verbosity is set correctly
rules.explanation: The log_error_verbosity GUC controls how much detail is included in logged error messages. Allowed values are TERSE, DEFAULT, and VERBOSE. TERSE omits DETAIL, HINT, QUERY, and CONTEXT; VERBOSE adds SQLSTATE and source location fields. The value should follow organizational logging policy.
rules.impact: Insufficient verbosity can omit fields needed for troubleshooting and investigation. Excessive verbosity can enlarge logs and increase the chance that sensitive context is retained longer than necessary.

rules.title: Log_hostname is set correctly
rules.explanation: The log_hostname GUC controls whether connection log messages include the client hostname in addition to the client IP address. When hostname logging is not required by policy, leaving the setting off avoids DNS lookups on every logged connection.
rules.impact: Enabling hostname resolution for every connection can add latency and load depending on DNS configuration. Logging only IP addresses remains usable for investigation and can be resolved later when hostnames are needed.

rules.title: Log_statement is set correctly
rules.explanation: The log_statement GUC selects which SQL statement classes are written to the server log. Valid values include none, ddl, mod, and all. A common baseline is ddl unless organizational policy requires broader statement logging such as mod or all.
rules.impact: Statement logging that aligns with security and audit policy supports later review of schema changes and other database activity. A value of none leaves little evidence of executed SQL for investigation.

rules.title: Log_timezone is set correctly
rules.explanation: The log_timezone GUC sets the time zone used for timestamps in log messages. The setting is cluster-wide so all sessions emit consistent log timestamps. GMT or UTC is commonly used unless organizational policy specifies another zone.
rules.impact: Inconsistent or unexpected log time zones can obscure when events occurred during incident review. This setting affects only log timestamps; it does not change the database session time zone used by SQL functions such as now().

rules.title: The pgAudit extension is enabled
rules.explanation: The pgAudit extension provides detailed session and object audit logging through the standard PostgreSQL logging facility. It is commonly used when organizations need finer-grained audit evidence than basic statement logging for regulatory or certification requirements.
rules.impact: Standard log_statement output records what a client requested but often lacks the relation-level detail auditors need. Without pgAudit, reconstructing who accessed or changed specific objects can require fragile parsing of statement text and may be incomplete.

rules.title: Sudo is configured for PostgreSQL administration
rules.explanation: Operating-system administration of PostgreSQL is typically performed by multiple authorized users who should not share an interactive postgres login. sudo can elevate a regular UNIX account to the postgres DBMS owner for controlled cluster administration while preserving accountability.
rules.impact: Without a controlled privilege-elevation path such as sudo, organizations may resort to shared superuser logins or overly broad file permissions. That weakens access control and makes authoritative auditing of administrative actions more difficult.

rules.title: Excessive administrative privileges are revoked
rules.explanation: PostgreSQL administrative capabilities such as creating roles, creating databases, and managing replication should be limited to superusers or other explicitly designated administrative roles. Ordinary application roles should receive only the minimum privileges required, commonly separated into DDL-oriented and DML-oriented roles.
rules.impact: Login roles with unnecessary CREATEDB, CREATEROLE, or similar administrative attributes can alter security boundaries, create unauthorized accounts, or disrupt service. Least-privilege role design reduces the blast radius of compromised application credentials.

rules.title: Unnecessary SECURITY DEFINER and elevated function privileges are revoked
rules.explanation: Functions, procedures, and triggers sometimes run with elevated rights (for example SECURITY DEFINER) so application logic can perform privileged operations. Execute rights on those objects should be granted only to authorized roles, and elevated definitions should be limited to cases that genuinely require them.
rules.impact: Unrestricted execute rights on elevated routines enable privilege escalation: callers can inherit capabilities beyond their assigned role. That can lead to unauthorized data access or modification through application and database logic.
rules.scope: Permission settings for used functions/modules in PostgreSQL

rules.title: Predefined PostgreSQL roles are used for privileged capabilities
rules.explanation: PostgreSQL provides predefined roles that grant commonly needed privileged capabilities without assigning full superuser rights. Administrators can GRANT those roles to users or other roles to provide narrowly scoped access to specific features and catalog information.
rules.impact: Using predefined roles instead of broad superuser grants supports least privilege. Overuse of superuser access increases the impact of account compromise and makes routine administration harder to constrain and audit.
rules.scope: Privilege and user role settings in PostgreSQL

rules.title: Local UNIX-domain socket authentication is configured correctly
rules.explanation: Local connections over a UNIX-domain socket can use peer authentication in pg_hba.conf, which maps the connecting operating-system user to a database role of the same name. When matching database roles exist, peer authentication provides a strong local access control model for tools such as psql.
rules.impact: Weak local authentication methods (for example trust) allow unauthorized local users to obtain database access without proving identity. Misconfigured local rules undermine host-based access control for the cluster.

rules.title: Host TCP/IP authentication is configured correctly
rules.explanation: Remote and TCP/IP client access is controlled by host rules in pg_hba.conf. Authentication methods such as scram-sha-256, cert, gss, sspi, pam, ldap, and radius may be used according to environment design; trust, password, and ident are inappropriate for remote logon, and md5 is weaker than scram-sha-256.
rules.impact: Untrusted or obsolete host authentication methods increase the risk of credential theft and unauthorized remote database access. Strong authentication on host lines is a primary network-facing control for PostgreSQL.

rules.title: Backend runtime parameters are configured securely
rules.explanation: PostgreSQL starts a backend process for each client session. Several session-scoped runtime parameters controlled in that backend context can affect logging, authentication timing, and planner behavior, and should be set to secure operational values.
rules.impact: Insecure backend settings can weaken audit trails, introduce avoidable delays, or enable unsafe diagnostic behavior. Misconfiguration can also contribute to denial-of-service conditions or obscure forensic evidence.

rules.title: Postmaster runtime parameters are configured securely
rules.explanation: The postmaster is the supervising PostgreSQL process that accepts connections and manages server-wide startup settings. Postmaster-context GUCs include networking and TLS-related parameters that apply to the server instance as a whole.
rules.impact: Misconfigured postmaster parameters can expose the server on unintended interfaces, weaken TLS protections, or leave other instance-wide controls unset. Those weaknesses affect every client connection to the cluster.

rules.title: SIGHUP runtime parameters are configured securely
rules.explanation: Some PostgreSQL runtime parameters take effect after a SIGHUP reload without a full restart. These settings commonly reside in postgresql.conf and pg_hba.conf and may also be changed with ALTER SYSTEM, which writes postgresql.auto.conf.
rules.impact: Incorrect SIGHUP-scoped settings can weaken logging, authentication, or related server behavior while appearing to require no restart. Superuser control of these parameters makes their secure baseline especially important.

rules.title: Superuser runtime parameters are configured securely
rules.explanation: Certain PostgreSQL GUCs may be changed only by a database superuser (traditionally the postgres role). These parameters are maintained in postgresql.conf or via ALTER SYSTEM into postgresql.auto.conf and influence logging and other privileged server behavior.
rules.impact: Insecure superuser-only settings can disable important integrity or audit controls across the cluster. Because only privileged roles can change them, establishing a secure baseline limits accidental or malicious weakening of those protections.

rules.title: User-level runtime parameters are configured securely
rules.explanation: Some PostgreSQL runtime parameters can be set at the role, session, or transaction level by ordinary users. These settings affect password hashing, transaction defaults, quoting behavior, and related session characteristics.
rules.impact: Unsafe user-settable defaults can weaken authentication material, alter isolation expectations, or introduce compatibility behaviors that increase risk. Establishing secure defaults reduces reliance on every role choosing safe values independently.

rules.title: FIPS 140-2 OpenSSL cryptography is used
rules.explanation: FIPS 140-2 validated OpenSSL provides approved cryptographic algorithms for protecting sensitive information. When PostgreSQL depends on OpenSSL for TLS or related cryptography, the host should use a FIPS-enabled OpenSSL configuration that meets organizational cryptographic policy.
rules.impact: Without FIPS-validated cryptography, the server may negotiate or use algorithms that do not meet organizational or regulatory requirements for confidentiality and integrity of protected data.
rules.scope: FIPS 140-2 OpenSSL settings in the OS for PostgreSQL

rules.title: SSL/TLS is enabled and configured correctly
rules.explanation: PostgreSQL can encrypt client and server TCP traffic with SSL/TLS when the ssl GUC is enabled and certificate and key files are configured. TLS protects authentication secrets and query data in transit between clients and the server.
rules.impact: If SSL/TLS is disabled or incompletely configured, database traffic may travel in cleartext on the network. That increases the risk of eavesdropping, credential theft, and tampering with data in transit.

rules.title: The pgcrypto extension is available
rules.explanation: The pgcrypto extension provides cryptographic SQL functions for hashing and encryption within PostgreSQL. It supports application and database designs that protect sensitive values at rest when field- or column-level cryptography is required.
rules.impact: Without suitable cryptographic facilities for data at rest, sensitive stored values may remain unprotected beyond filesystem or full-disk controls. Unauthorized disclosure or modification of that data becomes more likely if storage or backups are compromised.

rules.title: PostgreSQL configuration files reside outside the data directory
rules.explanation: By default, files such as postgresql.conf, pg_hba.conf, and pg_ident.conf may reside under the data directory ($PGDATA). PostgreSQL can relocate config_file, hba_file, and ident_file outside the data directory so ordinary superuser file access inside the cluster path cannot readily alter them. Include directories can still supply additional parameter fragments when needed.
rules.impact: Keeping primary configuration files inside the data directory increases the chance of accidental or intentional modification by anyone with broad access to cluster files. Separating configuration from data strengthens change control and reduces that risk.

rules.title: Selected PostgreSQL subdirectory locations reside outside the data directory
rules.explanation: A PostgreSQL cluster uses dedicated subdirectories for functions such as logging and write-ahead logging. For performance, reliability, and security, organizations often place those locations on separate filesystems or paths outside the primary data directory.
rules.impact: Leaving high-growth directories such as logs or WAL on the same volume as the data directory can allow runaway writes to fill the filesystem and interrupt the server. Separating them also limits unnecessary exposure of operational artifacts stored beside database files.

rules.title: PgBackRest is installed and configured
rules.explanation: pgBackRest is a PostgreSQL-focused backup and restore tool that implements its own backup protocol and features such as full, differential, and incremental backups, parallel transfer, encryption, and resume support. It is designed for reliable backup of large clusters without depending on generic tools such as tar or rsync.
rules.impact: Native utilities such as pg_dump and pg_basebackup cover important use cases but may not meet requirements for scalable, resumable, or encrypted physical backup workflows. Without a properly configured backup tool and process, recovery objectives and ransomware resilience are harder to meet.

rules.title: The pg_permissions extension is used to audit object privileges
rules.explanation: The pg_permissions extension lets administrators declare expected object privileges for database roles and report deviations from that policy. It presents privilege compliance in a form that is easier to review than raw catalog ACL output alone.
rules.impact: Manual privilege audits are error-prone in large schemas. Without a structured privilege baseline and reporting mechanism, excessive or missing grants are more likely to go unnoticed.

rules.title: The set_user extension is installed
rules.explanation: The set_user extension provides controlled, auditable privilege escalation to privileged roles inside PostgreSQL, similar in intent to sudo at the operating-system level. It is used to avoid direct day-to-day logins as a superuser while still allowing authorized elevation when required.
rules.impact: Direct shared use of the superuser role makes it difficult to attribute administrative actions to an individual. Without an elevation-and-audit model such as set_user, accountability for privileged database activity is weakened.
rules.scope: Settings in set_user extension in PostgreSQL

rules.title: Log_connections is enabled for backend sessions
rules.explanation: Backend-session logging of connection attempts is controlled by the log_connections GUC. When enabled, PostgreSQL records each connection attempt and successful authentication for later review.
rules.impact: Without log_connections, unexpected or failed session starts may leave little durable evidence. That reduces the effectiveness of access monitoring and incident investigation.

rules.title: Log_disconnections is enabled for backend sessions
rules.explanation: Backend-session logging of session termination is controlled by the log_disconnections GUC. When enabled, PostgreSQL records the end of each session and its duration.
rules.impact: Without log_disconnections, operators lose correlated end-of-session evidence for auditing. Long-running or abnormal sessions are harder to identify and investigate.

rules.title: Post_auth_delay is disabled
rules.explanation: The post_auth_delay GUC introduces an artificial pause after authentication succeeds and before a session begins normal work. It is intended only for debugging and should remain at 0 in production.
rules.impact: A non-zero post_auth_delay can degrade availability and be abused to slow client access after authentication. Leaving the delay enabled outside controlled troubleshooting increases operational risk.

rules.title: Event_source is set appropriately
rules.explanation: The event_source GUC sets the application identifier used when PostgreSQL logs to the Windows event log. On UNIX-like systems the setting is typically unused, but it should be reviewed where event-log destinations apply.
rules.impact: An incorrect event source name can make PostgreSQL messages harder to isolate in centralized Windows logging. That reduces the usefulness of event-log based monitoring and alerting.

rules.title: Listen_addresses is not set to a wildcard
rules.explanation: The listen_addresses GUC controls which TCP addresses the postmaster uses to accept client connections. Binding should be limited to required interfaces rather than an unrestricted wildcard such as *.
rules.impact: Listening on all interfaces unnecessarily expands the network attack surface. Clients on unintended networks may be able to reach the database port and attempt authentication.

rules.title: Logging_collector is enabled for the postmaster
rules.explanation: The logging_collector GUC starts the background process that captures stderr-based server messages into log files. It is a postmaster-start setting required for file-based logging destinations such as stderr and csvlog.
rules.impact: Without the collector, important server messages may not be retained in managed log files. That weakens operational monitoring and security auditing of the instance.

rules.title: The PostgreSQL port is explicitly configured
rules.explanation: The port GUC sets the TCP port on which the postmaster listens for client connections. An explicit, policy-approved port value should be configured for the instance.
rules.impact: An unset or unexpected port can hinder inventory, firewall, and monitoring controls that assume a known listener. Ambiguous listener configuration also complicates secure network exposure reviews.

rules.title: SSL is enabled
rules.explanation: The ssl GUC enables SSL/TLS support in the PostgreSQL server so eligible client connections can be encrypted. Enabling SSL is a prerequisite for protecting TCP database traffic with certificates and negotiated ciphers.
rules.impact: When SSL remains off, client connections may transmit credentials and query data without transport encryption. That increases exposure to network eavesdropping and related attacks.

rules.title: Ssl_ca_file is configured
rules.explanation: The ssl_ca_file GUC names the Certificate Authority certificate file used to verify client certificates when certificate-based TLS authentication or verification is required.
rules.impact: Without a configured CA file, the server cannot properly validate client certificates against a trusted authority. Certificate authentication and mutual TLS controls may fail open or be unavailable.

rules.title: Ssl_cert_file is configured
rules.explanation: The ssl_cert_file GUC specifies the server TLS certificate file presented to clients during the SSL handshake. The certificate path must be set for TLS-enabled PostgreSQL listeners.
rules.impact: A missing or incorrect server certificate prevents proper TLS negotiation. Clients may be unable to establish encrypted connections or may fall back to weaker trust models.

rules.title: Ssl_ciphers is configured securely
rules.explanation: The ssl_ciphers GUC defines the OpenSSL cipher list offered by PostgreSQL for TLS connections. The list should exclude weak constructs such as NULL, EXPORT, DES, RC4, and MD5-based ciphers.
rules.impact: Weak cipher suites allow attackers to downgrade or compromise transport confidentiality and integrity. A hardened cipher list reduces exposure to known cryptographic weaknesses.

rules.title: Ssl_crl_file is configured when certificate revocation is required
rules.explanation: The ssl_crl_file GUC points to a Certificate Revocation List used to reject revoked client or related certificates during TLS verification.
rules.impact: Without CRL checking where policy requires it, revoked certificates may continue to authenticate successfully. That prolongs access for compromised or retired credentials.

rules.title: Ssl_ecdh_curve is configured
rules.explanation: The ssl_ecdh_curve GUC selects the elliptic curve used for ECDH key exchange in TLS. A suitable curve such as prime256v1 should be configured; a value of none disables this mechanism.
rules.impact: Disabling or misconfiguring ECDH curves can weaken TLS key exchange strength or interoperability. Strong curve selection supports modern transport security for PostgreSQL connections.

rules.title: Ssl_key_file is configured
rules.explanation: The ssl_key_file GUC specifies the private key that corresponds to the server TLS certificate. The key file must be present and correctly referenced for SSL/TLS operation.
rules.impact: Without a valid private key, the server cannot complete TLS handshakes. Encrypted client connectivity and certificate-based server authentication will fail.

rules.title: Ssl_prefer_server_ciphers is enabled
rules.explanation: The ssl_prefer_server_ciphers GUC controls whether the server's cipher preference order takes precedence over the client's during TLS negotiation. Enabling it keeps cipher selection under server policy.
rules.impact: If clients dictate cipher order, they may negotiate weaker suites than organizational policy allows. Server preference helps enforce a consistent TLS baseline.

rules.title: Unix_socket_group is configured
rules.explanation: The unix_socket_group GUC sets the owning group of PostgreSQL UNIX-domain sockets. Defining a dedicated group supports group-restricted socket permissions for local clients.
rules.impact: An empty or unmanaged socket group makes it harder to limit local socket access to approved accounts. Broader local access increases the risk of unauthorized local connections.

rules.title: Unix_socket_permissions are restrictive
rules.explanation: The unix_socket_permissions GUC sets the permission mode on PostgreSQL UNIX-domain sockets. Restrictive modes such as 0770 or 0700 limit which local users can connect through the socket.
rules.impact: Overly permissive socket modes (for example 0777) allow any local user to attempt database connections on the socket. That expands local attack opportunities against authentication and application roles.

rules.title: Db_user_namespace is disabled
rules.explanation: The db_user_namespace GUC enables per-database user namespaces, a deprecated compatibility feature removed in newer PostgreSQL releases. Where the setting still exists, it should remain off.
rules.impact: Enabling db_user_namespace changes role-name interpretation in ways that complicate access control and compatibility. Keeping it disabled avoids unexpected authentication and privilege behavior.

rules.title: Krb_caseins_users is disabled
rules.explanation: The krb_caseins_users GUC controls whether Kerberos principal user-name matching is case-insensitive. Unless policy explicitly requires case-insensitive matching, the setting should remain off.
rules.impact: Case-insensitive Kerberos matching can cause distinct principals to map to the same database role unexpectedly. That may grant access beyond the intended identity mapping.

rules.title: Krb_server_keyfile is set when GSS/SSPI authentication is used
rules.explanation: The krb_server_keyfile GUC locates the Kerberos keytab (or equivalent) used by the server for GSSAPI/SSPI authentication. It must be configured when pg_hba.conf uses gss or sspi methods.
rules.impact: An empty key file location while GSS/SSPI rules are active can break secure Kerberos authentication or force weaker fallback behavior. Proper keytab configuration is required for those host authentication methods.

rules.title: Log_autovacuum_min_duration is configured
rules.explanation: The log_autovacuum_min_duration GUC controls when autovacuum actions are written to the server log. A value of -1 disables autovacuum logging; organizations typically set a non-negative threshold according to logging policy.
rules.impact: Disabling autovacuum logging removes visibility into maintenance activity that can affect performance and availability. Missing those records complicates operational troubleshooting and capacity analysis.

rules.title: Log_destination is configured for SIGHUP-managed logging
rules.explanation: The log_destination GUC selects active logging destinations such as stderr, csvlog, or syslog. The setting can be reloaded with SIGHUP and must remain populated for server logs to be retained.
rules.impact: Clearing or missetting log_destination can silently stop durable logging after a reload. Loss of logs reduces detection and investigation capability.

rules.title: Log_directory is configured for SIGHUP-managed logging
rules.explanation: The log_directory GUC defines where collector-managed log files are stored. It should point to an approved location consistent with organizational logging and retention practices.
rules.impact: An incorrect log directory can cause logging failures or place audit data where monitoring and access controls do not expect it. That undermines both availability of logs and their confidentiality.

rules.title: Log_file_mode is configured for SIGHUP-managed logging
rules.explanation: The log_file_mode GUC applies permission bits to files created by the logging collector. Restrictive modes limit read and write access to approved accounts only.
rules.impact: Permissive log file modes can disclose sensitive logged content to unauthorized local users. Tight permissions reduce that disclosure risk.

rules.title: Log_rotation_age is configured
rules.explanation: The log_rotation_age GUC sets the maximum age of an individual log file before time-based rotation occurs when the logging collector is enabled. A value of 0 disables time-based rotation.
rules.impact: Disabling time-based rotation can allow individual log files to grow without schedule-based boundaries. That complicates retention management and increases the chance of disk exhaustion.

rules.title: Log_timezone is configured
rules.explanation: The log_timezone GUC establishes the time zone embedded in log message timestamps. A deliberate cluster-wide value keeps log timelines consistent for operators and audit tooling.
rules.impact: Unset or inconsistent log time zones make event correlation across systems more difficult during incident response and compliance review.

rules.title: Syslog_facility is configured
rules.explanation: The syslog_facility GUC selects which syslog facility PostgreSQL uses when syslog logging is enabled. The facility should align with host syslog configuration and organizational routing rules.
rules.impact: An incorrect facility can misfile or drop PostgreSQL syslog records. That reduces the reliability of centralized logging pipelines.

rules.title: Syslog_ident is configured
rules.explanation: The syslog_ident GUC sets the program name tag attached to PostgreSQL messages in syslog, commonly postgres. The identifier should be set deliberately so messages can be filtered reliably.
rules.impact: A missing or incorrect syslog identity makes it harder to separate PostgreSQL events from other applications in aggregated logs.

rules.title: Ignore_checksum_failure is disabled
rules.explanation: The ignore_checksum_failure GUC controls whether PostgreSQL continues after detecting page checksum failures when data checksums are enabled. The setting should remain off so checksum failures are treated as errors.
rules.impact: Ignoring checksum failures can allow corrupted pages to be read as if they were valid. That risks silent data corruption and weakens integrity detection.

rules.title: Log_error_verbosity is configured
rules.explanation: The log_error_verbosity GUC, which only a superuser can change at the system level, controls how much detail appears in logged errors. The value should match organizational logging and privacy requirements.
rules.impact: Poorly chosen verbosity can either withhold investigative detail or retain excessive sensitive context in logs. Both extremes impair secure operations.

rules.title: Log_min_messages is configured
rules.explanation: The log_min_messages GUC sets the minimum message severity written to the server log. Superuser-managed defaults should capture security- and operations-relevant events without unnecessary debug noise.
rules.impact: An overly quiet threshold can hide warnings and errors needed for detection. An overly verbose threshold can overwhelm log storage and obscure important events.

rules.title: Log_statement is not set to none
rules.explanation: The log_statement GUC determines whether SQL statements are recorded in the server log. A value other than none is required when organizational policy expects statement-class auditing such as ddl, mod, or all.
rules.impact: With log_statement set to none, schema changes and other statement activity may leave little evidence in server logs. That weakens accountability and forensic reconstruction.

rules.title: Backslash_quote is set securely
rules.explanation: The backslash_quote GUC controls whether a backslash (\) is allowed to quote single-quote characters in string literals. Secure values are safe_encoding or off; allowing unrestricted backslash quoting increases compatibility risk.
rules.impact: Unsafe backslash quoting can create ambiguous string parsing behavior between clients and the server. That ambiguity has historically contributed to SQL injection and application logic errors.

rules.title: Default_transaction_isolation is set correctly
rules.explanation: The default_transaction_isolation GUC sets the isolation level used when a session does not request another level explicitly. read committed is a common baseline for general-purpose workloads unless policy requires a stricter level.
rules.impact: An unexpected default isolation level can change concurrency behavior and the visibility of uncommitted or concurrent data. Applications may then operate outside their assumed consistency model.

rules.title: Idle_in_transaction_session_timeout is configured
rules.explanation: The idle_in_transaction_session_timeout GUC terminates sessions that remain idle inside an open transaction longer than the configured limit. A value of 0 disables the timeout.
rules.impact: Sessions left idle in a transaction can hold locks and prevent VACUUM from cleaning dead rows. Disabling the timeout increases the risk of blocking, table bloat, and denial-of-service conditions.

rules.title: Password_encryption is set correctly
rules.explanation: The password_encryption GUC selects the algorithm used to store passwords in pg_authid for password-based authentication. scram-sha-256 is preferred on modern PostgreSQL releases; md5 is weaker and retained mainly for compatibility.
rules.impact: Weaker password storage formats make offline cracking easier if catalog contents are disclosed. Strong password_encryption settings improve resistance to credential compromise.

rules.title: Tcp_keepalives_idle is configured
rules.explanation: The tcp_keepalives_idle GUC specifies how long a TCP connection may remain idle before the operating system begins sending keepalive probes. Configuring keepalive behavior helps detect dead peers on persistent connections.
rules.impact: Without appropriate TCP keepalives, abandoned client connections may linger and continue to consume backend slots. That can reduce availability for legitimate sessions.

rules.title: The SSL CA certificate file is configured
rules.explanation: The ssl_ca_file GUC identifies the trusted Certificate Authority certificate used when PostgreSQL verifies client certificates. The file must be configured for TLS deployments that rely on certificate validation.
rules.impact: If the CA certificate path is missing, client-certificate verification cannot be performed reliably. Unauthorized clients may be accepted or legitimate certificate authentication may fail.

rules.title: The SSL server certificate file is configured
rules.explanation: The ssl_cert_file GUC specifies the server certificate presented during TLS handshakes. A valid certificate file is required for encrypted client connections to the database.
rules.impact: Without a correctly configured server certificate, TLS cannot be established as intended. Clients lose transport protection and may refuse to connect under secure policies.

rules.title: The SSL certificate revocation list file is configured
rules.explanation: The ssl_crl_file GUC points to the Certificate Revocation List consulted during TLS certificate verification. Configure it when organizational policy requires checking for revoked certificates.
rules.impact: Missing CRL configuration can allow revoked certificates to remain usable. Compromised or retired credentials may continue to authenticate until other controls intervene.

rules.title: The SSL server private key file is configured
rules.explanation: The ssl_key_file GUC specifies the private key associated with the server TLS certificate. The key must be present, protected by filesystem permissions, and correctly referenced in PostgreSQL.
rules.impact: An absent or incorrect private key prevents successful TLS operation. Encrypted connectivity and server authentication depend on this material being configured correctly.

rules.title: Log_directory is located outside the data directory
rules.explanation: The log_directory GUC should reference a location outside the primary data directory when organizational policy relocates logs for security and operations. Absolute paths outside $PGDATA are preferred over relative paths such as log or pg_log.
rules.impact: Keeping logs inside the data directory mixes audit artifacts with database files and can allow log growth to consume the same filesystem the cluster needs to remain online.

rules.title: Log_filename uses a proper naming template
rules.explanation: The log_filename GUC defines the naming pattern for collector-managed log files. The value is processed as a strftime template, so time-based %-substitutions should be used unless another controlled rotation scheme is in place.
rules.impact: A static file name without rotation can cause a single log file to grow without bound or to be overwritten unpredictably. That risks disk exhaustion and loss of audit history.

rules.title: Log_truncate_on_rotation is enabled
rules.explanation: When the logging collector is enabled, log_truncate_on_rotation controls whether PostgreSQL truncates an existing log file of the same name during scheduled rotation instead of appending indefinitely. Truncation applies to time-based schedule opens rather than startup or size-based rotation alone.
rules.impact: With truncation disabled and recurring file names, log data can accumulate without bound in the same files. That complicates analysis and increases the likelihood of filling the log volume.

rules.title: Log_rotation_age is set correctly
rules.explanation: The log_rotation_age GUC sets the maximum lifetime of a log file before automatic time-based rotation when the logging collector is enabled. The interval should follow organizational retention and review practices.
rules.impact: An excessive interval or a value of 0 (disabled) can leave log files open too long. That raises the risk of oversized files, harder reviews, and potential loss of manageable audit segments.

rules.title: Log_rotation_size is set correctly
rules.explanation: The log_rotation_size GUC sets the maximum size of an individual log file before size-based rotation occurs. A positive limit should be configured in line with organizational logging policy.
rules.impact: A value of 0 disables size-based rotation. Combined with weak time-based rotation, log files may grow without bound and threaten disk space or logging continuity.

rules.title: Syslog_ident is set correctly
rules.explanation: The syslog_ident GUC defines the program name used to tag PostgreSQL messages in syslog (for example postgres). The identifier should be set consistently with organizational log-parsing rules.
rules.impact: An incorrect syslog_ident value makes it difficult to isolate PostgreSQL events from other syslog traffic during monitoring and incident response.

rules.title: Debug_pretty_print is enabled
rules.explanation: The debug_pretty_print GUC formats output from debug_print_parse, debug_print_rewritten, and debug_print_plan with indentation when those debug settings are enabled. It improves readability of diagnostic parse and plan logs.
rules.impact: When debug printing is required by policy but pretty printing is off, logs use a compact format that is harder to review. That slows analysis of authorized diagnostic output.

rules.title: Excessive DML privileges are revoked
rules.explanation: Table-level DML privileges such as INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, and TRUNCATE should be granted only to authorized roles. PostgreSQL enforces these rights through GRANT and REVOKE at the object level, and PUBLIC should not retain unnecessary DML grants.
rules.impact: Excessive DML privileges allow unauthorized users or roles to modify or destroy data. Reducing grants to the minimum required limits the impact of compromised application accounts.

rules.title: WAL archiving is configured
rules.explanation: Write-ahead log (WAL) archiving copies completed WAL segments to standby or backup storage for point-in-time recovery. PostgreSQL controls this behavior with archive_mode and archive_command (or equivalent archiving configuration in supported versions).
rules.impact: Without working WAL archiving, point-in-time recovery and continuous backup pipelines may be unavailable. Recovery options after corruption, operator error, or disaster are then severely limited.
